questions.question: Name and explain five clues used to interpret satellite images, and list the four things to check before starting.
questions.expected_answer: Tone and colour: how light, dark or what colour a feature is, such as dark water and white cloud. Texture: how smooth or rough it looks, such as a smooth dam and a rough forest. Shape: human features have straight lines and regular shapes, natural features irregular ones. Size: judged against the scale, such as a farm dam versus a reservoir. Pattern: the arrangement, such as a grid of suburbs or a patchwork of fields. Also shadow and location or association. Checks before starting: direction of north, scale or resolution, date, and whether the image is true or false colour.

questions.question: Explain how water, natural forest, timber plantations and centre-pivot irrigation can be identified on satellite images.
questions.expected_answer: Water is very dark blue or black in true colour because it absorbs light, and very dark in false colour because it absorbs near-infrared; muddy water is brown; dams have a straight edge at the wall and branching arms up valleys. Natural forest is dark green with a rough, mottled texture and irregular edges. Timber plantations are also dark but form neat blocks with straight edges and firebreaks. Centre-pivot irrigation appears as bright green circles, often several hundred metres across, standing out against dry land, as along the Orange River.

questions.question: Describe how a cold front, thunderstorms, a tropical cyclone and coastal fog appear on weather satellite images, and explain how infrared images are read.
questions.expected_answer: A cold front is a long curved band of cloud, often hundreds of kilometres long, moving eastwards from the ocean south-west of South Africa. Thunderstorms are bright white rounded clusters, often over the Highveld on summer afternoons. A tropical cyclone is a huge spiral of cloud with a clear eye, turning clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Coastal fog is a smooth, flat grey-white sheet with sharp edges along the cold west coast. Infrared images show temperature: the brighter the white, the colder and usually higher the cloud top, which often means heavier rain.
